The Estate

Some houses hold history.
This one shaped it.

Neo-Georgian. Four columns. Seven fireplaces. Built in 1916 by the men who built Pinehurst.

Built by Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen.
The same men who built Pinehurst.

Four columns. Full entablature. Drawn to exact Georgian proportion and built that way. The proportions are correct because the drawings survived.

200 Hollycrest Drive

The gate has been here
longer than the road.

Wrought iron. Original hardware. This is where arrival begins — before the door, before the columns, before the house announces itself.

The Threshold

The door has been open
since 1916.

The leaded glass sidelights and fanlight are original. The hardware was specified in 1916. It has not been replaced.

The Entry Hall

The central axis runs
straight through.

Original oak floors. The staircase rises at the far end — visible the instant the door opens. No wall has moved.

In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.

The Drawing Room

Fire going,
no one home yet.

The Delft tile surround — blue and white, hand-painted — is original. The toile was sourced to match it. A century of conviction.

The Dining Room

The shell cabinets
were already there.
They are still there now.

The frontispiece above the fireplace is original — carved in 1916, still in place. The shell cabinets have not moved. The arched niche, the wainscoting, the brass chandelier: all of it was here or was rebuilt to match what was.

The room seats twelve without crowding. It holds the silence after dinner without trying.

The shell cabinets are original. The kitchen is not. Both are right.

The Kitchen

The only room rebuilt
from scratch. Done correctly.

Reclaimed heart-pine floors — the only room in the house not original oak. Custom white cabinetry. Dark granite. Three south-facing windows over the sink.

The Library

The room the man who founded Doubleday
would have claimed.

Dead center of the first floor — positioned that way in the 2000 plans. Built-in shelving on three walls, floor to ceiling. Rolling ladder. French doors to the rear grounds.

O'Shea designed this room to the same standard as the 1916 house it joined. When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

Thomas O'Shea, Architect · Durham, NC · January 2000

"Renovations and Additions."
His word choice tells you everything.

Fifteen sheets of drawings. Every profile matched. Every cornice detail copied from what was already there. The result does not feel added. It feels inevitable.

The hardware was specified in 1916.
It has not been replaced.

The Primary Suite

The master suite was a commission,
not a renovation.

Every panel, every cabinet, the fireplace surround, the tub surround — drawn from scratch in 2000 to match a house built 84 years earlier. You cannot tell the difference. That was the point.

The dogwood blooms every April. The window has not moved.

Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918

Editor. Publisher. Ambassador.
The man who built Garran Hill
and never slept here.

Walter Hines Page bought 1,000 acres outside Pinehurst in February 1913 and named it Garran Hill. Six weeks later, Woodrow Wilson made him Ambassador to the Court of St. James. He sailed for London in May 1913.

His son Ralph supervised construction using Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen. The house was complete by 1916. From London, Page wrote about it constantly.

"The farm — the farm — the farm."
Walter Hines Page · Letters from London · 1914–1918

He served through the First World War. He returned in December 1918, carried off the train at Aberdeen by his son. His last words were spoken at Pinehurst, not at Garran Hill.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"
Walter Hines Page · Pinehurst, December 1918 · His last words
Westminster Abbey · Memorial Inscription · 1918 "The friend of Britain in her sorest need."

The Grounds

The world outside these gates
does not exist here.

4.15 acres enclosed within mature hardwoods. All utilities underground.

The Pool

20 by 40. Salt water. Converted 2022. Original brick surround. Wrought iron arch gate. Hidden entirely behind the rose wall. You cannot see it from the road. You cannot hear the road from it.

The Garden

28-zone irrigation from a 130-foot private well. Three American sycamores planted by Betty Dumaine in 1959. The camellia garden was hers. Long-leaf pines are descendants of the forest cleared by Frank Page's logging.

The Infrastructure

All utilities underground. 130-foot private well, 80-gallon storage tank. 28 irrigation zones. 12+ parking spaces. The grounds function without effort because they were engineered to.

Betty Dumaine kept foxhounds here.
And peacocks. And one Irish Hunter named Blue Fox.

He is buried at the rear of the property, under a slate cover with a brass marker. A four-foot blue fox statue once marked the grave. It was lost after her death in 1980. The marker is still there.

Someone still puts flowers there.

Stewardship

She planted this garden from scratch.
This is what twenty years of care looks like.

Betty Dumaine purchased Garran Hill in 1959. She left it to Duke University when she died in 1980. The house stood vacant for sixteen years. In 1998, the current stewards purchased it. Thomas O'Shea began the restoration in 1999. They moved in late 2001.

"We fell in love with its character, its history, and the way it felt the moment we walked through the door."

Current Stewards · Garran Hill · 2001 – Present
